title: A Clever Manager and a Beggar
overview: Jesus tells two stories about wealth, one about a fired manager who plans ahead and one about a rich man who ignores a beggar, with sayings in between about money, honesty and the Law.

parts.label: A manager about to be fired (vv. 1-8)
parts.note: Caught wasting his boss's property, the manager cuts one debtor's bill in half and another's by a fifth, so they will take him in once he loses his job. The boss praises his foresight, not his honesty; many read the cuts as one last cheat, while some scholars think he dropped only his own commission or hidden interest.

parts.label: Lessons about money (vv. 9-13)
parts.note: Jesus draws the lesson that money will not last, so use it now to make friends, which many take to mean helping the poor, and you will be welcomed into eternal homes. How someone handles small things like money shows whether they can be trusted with what truly matters, and no one can serve both God and money as their master.

parts.label: A reply to scoffers (vv. 14-15)
parts.note: Luke says the Pharisees listening, members of a respected religious movement, loved money and sneered at this teaching. Jesus replies that looking upright to others means little, because God sees the heart, and much that people prize is offensive to God.

parts.label: The Law still stands (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Jesus says the Law and the Prophets, meaning the Jewish Scriptures, led up to John the Baptist, and since then God's kingdom is being announced, though scholars debate what verse 16 means by people forcing their way in. Yet the Law keeps its force, and he says divorcing and remarrying counts as adultery, a stricter rule than was common then, which Christians still apply in different ways.

parts.label: A rich man and a beggar (vv. 19-26)
parts.note: A rich man dressed in purple, a costly dye worn by royalty, feasts every day while Lazarus, starving and covered in sores, lies at his gate. After both die their places are reversed: Lazarus is comforted beside Abraham, a Jewish picture of the honoured dead, while the rich man is in agony in Hades, the realm of the dead, across a gap no one can cross.

parts.label: A warning for five brothers (vv. 27-31)
parts.note: The rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers, but Abraham says they already have Moses and the Prophets, the Jewish Scriptures, which teach care for the poor. If they ignore those, he says, even someone rising from the dead will not convince them, a line Christians have long read as pointing toward Jesus' resurrection.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the story of the rich man and Lazarus describes what really happens after death or is a parable that borrows familiar Jewish pictures of the afterlife to make a point about wealth and neglect.
think: What do you think makes it possible to pass the same person in need day after day and stop really seeing them?
